encounters.cc: Chronic fatigue and intermittent jaundice, with recent scleral icterus following viral illness last year.

lines: Chronic fatigue and intermittent jaundice, with recent scleral icterus following viral illness last year.
The patient is a 17-year-old male with hereditary spherocytosis, Wilson disease, and cystinuria who returns for follow-up, last evaluated in January 2020.
He has felt more tired than his peers since childhood and frequently requires breaks during sports.
His parents report that he had mild scleral icterus during a viral illness last year, which resolved spontaneously.
He denies bleeding, fever, weight loss, or recent medication use.
He has never required a transfusion.
Past labs from several years ago showed mild anemia, but no specific follow-up was done.
- Bilateral nephrostomy tube placement (age 14, for obstructing cystine stones)
- Zinc acetate 50 mg three times daily
Family history is notable for his father undergoing splenectomy and cholecystectomy in his twenties for similar symptoms.
The father has had no symptoms since those surgeries.
Smoking: Never. Alcohol: None. Occupation: High school student.
Physical examination today reveals mild scleral icterus, pale conjunctivae, and splenomegaly.
There is no hepatomegaly, rash, or lymphadenopathy.
Neurologic and cardiopulmonary exams are unremarkable.
Laboratory studies reveal normocytic anemia, elevated lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), low haptoglobin, and indirect hyperbilirubinemia.
Peripheral blood smear demonstrates small, round red cells without central pallor.
An osmotic fragility test is positive.
Flow cytometry with eosin-5-maleimide binding shows decreased fluorescence intensity in the patient's erythrocytes compared to controls.

encounters.cc: Progressive clumsiness, mood changes, hand tremors, and yellowing of the eyes over the past 6 months.

lines: Progressive clumsiness, mood changes, hand tremors, and yellowing of the eyes over the past 6 months.
The patient presents for neurological evaluation in the context of known hereditary spherocytosis managed in Hematology in January and May 2020.
He has become more irritable, withdrawn from friends, and his grades have dropped noticeably.
The parents have noticed occasional hand tremors and difficulty with handwriting.
Over the past year, he has had intermittent jaundice and episodes of dark urine without pain.
- Bilateral nephrostomy tube placement (age 14, for obstructing cystine stones)
- Zinc acetate 50 mg three times daily
The patient's father recalls that his brother died in his twenties from liver failure of unclear cause.
He denies alcohol or illicit drug use.
There is no history of blood transfusions, significant travel, or hepatotoxic medication use.
Physical examination reveals mild scleral icterus and hepatomegaly on abdominal palpation without splenomegaly.
Neurologic exam shows a fine resting tremor, mild dysarthria, and slowed rapid alternating movements, but normal strength.
His gait is slightly wide-based but stable.
The patient is hemodynamically stable and is able to swallow oral medications without difficulty.
Laboratory evaluation shows evidence of hemolytic anemia and mildly prolonged prothrombin time.
Serum ceruloplasmin is markedly reduced, and a 24-hour urinary copper excretion is elevated.
Brain MRI reveals symmetric hyperintensities in the basal ganglia.

lines: Persistent jaundice and fatigue for the past two months that has not resolved as in previous episodes.

He has been seen previously in Hematology and the emergency department for similar presentations.
He reports fatigue and a yellowish tinge to his skin and eyes for the past two months.
His parents add that he has had several episodes of jaundice since infancy, usually following an illness, but the jaundice would resolve on its own.
This time, however, it has persisted.
He denies abdominal pain, but does report feeling full quickly after eating.
His past medical history is significant for cholecystectomy at age 12 due to gallstones.
- Bilateral nephrostomy tube placement (age 14, for obstructing cystine stones)
- Zinc acetate 50 mg three times daily
- Mother: Asymptomatic carrier for Wilson disease and cystinuria
- Maternal uncle: Wilson disease (deceased from liver failure)
